A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PEFT meta-learning framework and core linear-model landscape results. Renamed methods and relocated material can be matched, and both versions' text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 report original synthetic linear-regression and RoBERTa-Large/ConvAI2 experiments. Appendix D.2 also reports numerical evidence of spurious local minima.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices D–F report original linear and shallow-network experiments, CIFAR-10 and ConvAI2 evaluations, and numerical optimization-landscape results.

M1.justification: V2 adds a Last-Layer-ML instantiation that adapts only the final layer, alongside LoRA. The generic base-weight/adapter objective remains unchanged under the Meta-Adapters/Meta-LoRA to PEFT-ML/LoRA-ML renaming. Algorithm 1 primarily documents optimization of the existing framework.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic linear regression and ConvAI2 conversation-continuation selection. V2 retains these and adds CIFAR-10 binary image-classification tasks and nonlinear scalar-regression data generated by shallow sigmoid networks, substantially broadening the evaluated domains and task relationships.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares Meta-LoRA against standard retraining followed by LoRA. V2 adds Reptile+LoRA to the ConvAI2 comparisons and evaluates SR+Last-Layer and Reptile+Last-Layer against Last-Layer-ML. The expanded comparator family also appears in the new CIFAR-10 evaluation.

E3.justification: ConvAI2 changes from RoBERTa-Large to RoBERTa-base, from 30 to 10 training epochs, and from best-heldout-epoch to last-epoch fine-tuning results. Batch sizes and learning rates also change (v1 Appendix C; v2 Appendix E.2). Synthetic evaluation changes from population loss to a stated sample prediction error, while the new vision experiments introduce paired-class tasks and image augmentation.

E4.justification: V2 adds synthetic adaptation-rank sensitivity and shallow-network sweeps over task count, sample counts, rank and dimension. ConvAI2's rank-8 retraining/rank-16 fine-tuning investigation is replaced by a matched-rank sweep over 1, 4, 8 and 16. The earlier spurious-local-minima analysis is retained in Appendix F rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 reports language-result medians across five trials without uncertainty estimates. V2 retains five language trials but reports means and standard errors, explicitly reports five-trial linear averages with full-range shading, and introduces ten-trial shallow-network medians with ranges covering the central six outcomes. This substantially changes statistical reporting, without establishing an increased ConvAI2 run count.

E6.justification: ConvAI2 results are replaced: v1 Table 1a reports 45.76 for Meta-LoRA-8 and 41.52 for SR+LoRA; v2 Table 2 reports 47.4 ± 1.9 and 35.0 ± 4.1 under revised settings. New CIFAR-10 results include 86.09 for LoRA-ML, 85.29 for SR+LoRA and 81.30 for Reptile+LoRA. Shallow-network and additional rank-sweep results are also added. These are not controlled cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 adds finite-test-sample prediction bounds and corollaries, quantitative standard-retraining loss results, and asymmetric-adapter analysis in Appendix C. Retraining theory still assumes infinite samples. It also relaxes the requirement that all task-adapter columns be jointly independent and states explicit dimension conditions for the retained recovery and stationarity theorems. The core landscape proofs remain.

C1.justification: Beyond v1's population-level recovery and adaptability claims, v2's contributions assert finite-sample O(kd/n) adaptation rates and a task-dependent disadvantage for standard retraining. The abstract, introduction and conclusion also expand the empirical success claim from LoRA language adaptation to vision tasks and last-layer fine-tuning.

C2.justification: V2 attributes Reptile's poorer performance to mismatch between gradient-based adaptation and PEFT at test time, discusses shallow-network variability and outliers, and analyzes when zero-mean asymmetric adapters could allow standard retraining to recover shared parameters. It replaces v1's interpretation favoring larger fine-tuning than retraining rank with an interpretation of robustness across matched ranks.

D1.justification: V2 adds synthetic inner/outer optimization schedules, expanded hyperparameter tables, MLP-Mixer architecture and preprocessing details, language-head/tokenizer/loss descriptions, asset information and training pseudocode. Real-data hardware changes from an A40 to an H200. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although v1's average per-persona sample counts are no longer stated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Reptile, Saunshi et al., reduced-rank-regression and minimax references, and CIFAR-10/MLP-Mixer references; Mirsky is removed. It sharpens the distinction from shared-subspace meta-learning and connects LoRA fitting to reduced-rank regression. These are targeted extensions of largely retained PEFT research positioning; publication-year updates alone are not substantive additions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, and method terminology changes throughout. Main-text proof sketches are removed while full proofs remain in Appendix B. Experiments become a compact overview supported by reorganized and expanded appendices. This substantially changes the exposition and organization of retained material.

P2.justification: V1's four-panel Figure 1 becomes a two-panel main figure with expanded appendix plots. V2 adds shallow-network figures, vision tables, redesigned language comparisons and a pseudocode display, while repeating some main results in the appendices. The original spurious-minimum plot is retained as Figure 12. Figures 8 and 9 incorrectly reuse an identical plot under different sample-count captions.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the general PEFT framework through another adaptation method, Reptile comparisons, vision and nonlinear tasks, and explicit uncertainty reporting. Finite-test-sample analysis and considerably fuller implementation documentation address important theoretical and reproducibility gaps in v1. Revised ConvAI2 settings prevent direct accuracy comparisons, and the duplicated Figures 8–9 weaken one supplementary analysis, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and assessability.
